d: Explains physical assemblies and how they behave in Roblox's rigid body physics engine.
h:
An assembly is one or more parts welded by a rigid WeldConstraint or connected through movable joints, like Motor6Ds. You can group an assembly of parts in a model container to quickly organize the parts and related objects as a single asset.

<img src="../assets/physics/assemblies/Assembly-Example-Block.png" alt="A light blue cube against a dark blue background that represents an assembly of 1 part." width="100%" />
<figcaption>1 assembly; 1 part</figcaption>

<img src="../assets/physics/assemblies/Assembly-Example-Avatar.png" alt="A humanoid character model against a dark blue background that represents an assembly of 18 parts." width="100%" />
<figcaption>1 assembly; 18 parts</figcaption>

<img src="../assets/physics/assemblies/Assembly-Example-Ship.png" alt="A pirate that represents an assemble of 179 parts." width="100%" />
<figcaption>1 assembly; 179 parts</figcaption>


From a physics perspective, an assembly is considered a single rigid body, meaning no force can push or pull the connected parts from each other, and they will move as a single unit. All forces applied to a specific BasePart are applied to its assembly — for instance, BasePart:ApplyImpulse() applies impulse to the assembly at BasePart.AssemblyCenterOfMass.

The joints that combine multiple parts into assemblies are only active in the Workspace or another WorldModel instance. If the parts are stored elsewhere, all of the welds/connections that combine parts into assemblies will be non-functional.

To view colored outlines around parts in order to visualize single rigid body assemblies, toggle on Assemblies from the Visualization Options widget in the upper‑right corner of the 3D viewport.

Assembly properties

The following BasePart properties show data regarding its assembly. Their values will be the same for any part in the same assembly, so it doesn't matter which part you use.

Property Description
BasePart.AssemblyLinearVelocity The linear velocity vector of the part's assembly. Setting the velocity directly may lead to unrealistic motion, so usage of a VectorForce or LinearVelocity constraint is preferred, or BasePart:ApplyImpulse() for an instantaneous change in linear velocity.
BasePart.AssemblyAngularVelocity The angular velocity vector of the part's assembly. Setting the velocity directly may lead to unrealistic motion, so usage of a Torque or AngularVelocity constraint is preferred, or BasePart:ApplyAngularImpulse() for an instantaneous change in angular velocity.
BasePart.AssemblyCenterOfMass A read-only position calculated via the mass and position of all the parts in the assembly. A force applied to the center of mass will not cause angular acceleration, only linear.
BasePart.AssemblyMass The sum of the BasePart.Mass of all parts in the assembly. If the assembly has an anchored part, the assembly's mass is considered infinite.
BasePart.AssemblyRootPart The part automatically chosen to represent the assembly's [root part](#assembly-root-part).

Assembly root part

Every assembly has a root part indicated by its AssemblyRootPart property. This is the part that doesn't move when Motor6D transforms are updated, as well as the part used to keep consistent physics replication and network ownership.

You cannot explicitly set the root part, but the following factors affect probability from highest to lowest:

<div class="gcell" markdown="1"><img src="../assets/misc/Arrow-Higher.png" alt="" width="50" />

<div class="gcell" markdown="1">
An Anchored part will always be assigned as the root part.
</div>

<div class="gcell" markdown="1"><img src="../assets/misc/Arrow-High.png" alt="" width="50" />

<div class="gcell" markdown="1">
Parts with Massless set to **false** (default) take precedence.
</div>

<div class="gcell" markdown="1"><img src="../assets/misc/Arrow-Low.png" alt="" width="50" />

<div class="gcell" markdown="1">
Higher RootPriority values take precedence.
</div>

<div class="gcell" markdown="1"><img src="../assets/misc/Arrow-Lower.png" alt="" width="50" />

<div class="gcell" markdown="1">
Precedence based on the part's size (largest face area), with multipliers for specific part types. Seats and VehicleSeats receive the highest multiplier, followed by parts named **HumanoidRootPart**, then parts named **Torso**.
</div>

Anchoring behavior

When one of an assembly's parts is anchored, that part becomes the root part and all of the other parts become implicitly anchored with it. The following sequence illustrates this behavior.

  1. Below, four parts are welded together with WeldConstraints (green bars) to form a single assembly, as indicated by the matching colored outlines.
  1. If just one part in the assembly is anchored, the assembly will not change, other than the root part potentially changing (the anchored part always has the highest priority for becoming the root part).
  1. If more than one part is anchored, the assembly will split. Below, both the left and top parts are anchored, so the original assembly splits into two assemblies as shown by the colored outlines. Also, the WeldConstraint between the two assemblies deactivates, since you cannot have an active weld between two anchored assemblies.
If you want to anchor all parts in an assembly, you only need to anchor the assembly's root part. Anchoring all parts is actually less performant, as it creates more assemblies.

kid.simple: An assembly is a group of parts that are stuck together so the physics engine moves them as one single object. A lone block is an assembly of 1 part, your avatar is 1 assembly of 18 parts, and a ship can be 1 assembly of 179 parts. This matters because any push you give to one part moves the whole assembly, and anchoring one part can freeze the whole thing. Understanding assemblies helps you build vehicles, doors and machines that do not fall apart.
kid.analogy: A Lego spaceship you glued together is one assembly. If you push the wing, the whole ship slides, not just the wing. Gluing a single brick of the ship to the table holds the entire ship still.
keyPoints: An assembly is one or more parts joined by WeldConstraints or by movable joints like Motor6Ds.
Physics treats an assembly as one rigid body: its parts cannot be pulled apart and they always move together.
A force or impulse on any part is applied to the whole assembly. `ApplyImpulse` pushes the assembly at its center of mass.
Assembly properties like `AssemblyMass`, `AssemblyLinearVelocity` and `AssemblyCenterOfMass` give the same value no matter which part of the assembly you read them from.

Every assembly has a root part. You cannot pick it directly, but an anchored part always wins, then non-massless parts, then higher `RootPriority`, then bigger parts (Seats and parts named HumanoidRootPart get a boost).
Anchoring one part of an assembly anchors the whole thing. Anchoring two or more parts splits it into separate assemblies and turns off the weld between them.
To anchor a whole assembly, anchor only its root part. Anchoring every part is slower because it creates more assemblies.
Joints only work in the Workspace (or another WorldModel). Welded parts stored in, say, ServerStorage are not acting as an assembly.

terms.assembly: Parts joined together that physics moves as one object. Two 4x1x2 blocks welded side by side are 1 assembly, not 2.
terms.rigid body: A solid object that cannot bend or come apart. However hard you hit it, the parts keep the same distance from each other.
terms.WeldConstraint: An invisible glue that locks two parts together in their current positions.
terms.Motor6D: A joint that holds two parts together but can be animated to turn, like an avatar's shoulder.
terms.mass: How heavy something is. In Roblox, mass = volume x density. A 4x1x2 Plastic block has volume 8 and Plastic density 0.7, so its mass is 5.6.
terms.AssemblyMass: All the parts' masses added up. Two 5.6 blocks welded together have an `AssemblyMass` of 11.2. If any part is anchored, the mass counts as infinite.
terms.center of mass: The balance point of the whole assembly. Push exactly there and it slides without spinning; push off to the side and it also starts to spin.
terms.impulse: A sudden one-time shove. The speed change equals impulse divided by mass: an impulse of 112 upward on a mass of 11.2 adds 10 studs per second of upward speed.
terms.linear velocity: Speed plus direction, in studs per second. `Vector3.new(0, 0, -20)` means moving 20 studs per second toward negative Z.
terms.angular velocity: How fast it spins and around which axis, in radians per second. About 6.28 radians is one full turn.
terms.root part: The one part that represents the assembly. It stays put when Motor6Ds animate other parts, and it is used for network ownership.
terms.RootPriority: A number you can set on a part to make it more (higher number) or less likely to be chosen as root part.
terms.Massless: When true, the part adds no weight to its assembly (as long as it is not the root part).
terms.implicitly anchored: Not anchored itself, but frozen anyway because it is welded to a part that is anchored.
terms.WorldModel: A special container (like the Workspace) where physics and joints actually run.

example.title: Weld two blocks into one assembly and launch it
example.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local function makeBlock(position)
	local block = Instance.new("Part")
	block.Size = Vector3.new(4, 1, 2)        -- volume = 4 * 1 * 2 = 8
	block.Material = Enum.Material.Plastic   -- density 0.7, so mass = 5.6
	block.Position = position
	block.Parent = Workspace
	return block
end

local left = makeBlock(Vector3.new(0, 5, 0))
local right = makeBlock(Vector3.new(4, 5, 0))  -- right next to the first one

-- Glue them together so they become ONE assembly
local weld = Instance.new("WeldConstraint")
weld.Part0 = left
weld.Part1 = right
weld.Parent = left

task.wait(1)
print("Mass of left alone:", left.Mass)              -- about 5.6
print("Assembly mass:", left.AssemblyMass)           -- about 11.2
print("Same from right:", right.AssemblyMass)        -- also about 11.2
print("Root part:", left.AssemblyRootPart.Name)

-- Push only the LEFT part. The whole assembly flies up.
-- Speed change = impulse / mass = 112 / 11.2 = 10 studs per second
left:ApplyImpulse(Vector3.new(0, 112, 0))
explain: Each block is 4 x 1 x 2 = 8 cubic studs. Plastic has a density of 0.7, so each block's mass is 8 x 0.7 = 5.6.
The WeldConstraint joins the blocks, so the engine now sees one assembly with `AssemblyMass` 5.6 + 5.6 = 11.2. Reading it from either block gives the same number.
`AssemblyRootPart` tells you which block the engine picked as the root. Both are the same size and neither is anchored, so it could be either one.
`ApplyImpulse` on just the left block still moves both, because forces go to the whole assembly. An impulse of 112 divided by 11.2 mass adds 10 studs per second of upward speed.
If you change the impulse to 224, the upward speed change doubles to 20. If you add a third block (mass 16.8 total), the same 112 impulse only adds about 6.7.

watchOut: Setting `AssemblyLinearVelocity` directly every frame can look jerky and unrealistic. Prefer `ApplyImpulse` for a one-time kick, or constraints like LinearVelocity or VectorForce for steady pushes.
Anchoring every part of a building is slower than anchoring just one root part. Weld the pieces and anchor one.
Anchoring two parts in the same assembly splits it, and the weld between them stops working. Do not be surprised if the middle pieces suddenly act separately.
Welds do not work while parts sit in ServerStorage or ReplicatedStorage. They only become an assembly once they are in the Workspace.
You cannot set the root part directly. If you need a specific one, use `RootPriority` or make other parts `Massless`.
